newsitem.title: USA: Koch family feud set to head for trial next year.
newsitem.headline: Koch family feud set to head for trial next year.

text.p: A bitter feud between members of the wealthy Koch family looks set to go to trial next year after a federal judge ruled that some of the claims lacked merit but others could proceed, a plaintiffs lawyer said Wednesday.
"I think chances of a settlement now are remote," said lawyer Don Scott of Bartlit Beck, the Chicago firm representing the plaintiffs, William and Frederick Koch and the Simmons, Koch family cousins.

The dispute dates to 1983 when the plaintiffs agreed to sell out their interests in Koch Industries for $1.1 billion after falling out with Charles, chairman and chief executive officer of the Wichita, Kan.-based oil services company, the second-largest privately held company in the United States.
U.S. District Court Judge Sam Crow ruled on Friday that the plaintiffs could pursue three of 12 claims against Charles, brother David, Koch Industries and other Koch executives.
Koch Industries, in a statement on Tuesday evening, characterised the judge's ruling as a victory.
"The court ruled that, as a matter of law, there is no basis for 75 percent of William Koch's claims," Don Cordes, a Koch Industries executive vice president, said in the statement.
But Judge Crow ruled that three claims could proceed and those account for about two-thirds of the plantiffs' claim, Scott said.

"Our claim is still for over $300 million of actual damages as of June 1983, on top of which there is 15 years of pre-judgment interest and punitive damages in an amount to be determined," Scott said, adding the claim could be worth more than $1 billion.
The claim alleges that Charles and Koch Industries withheld information which they were legally required to disclose, leading to an undervaluation of the plaintiffs' company stock, Scott said.

Judge Crow heard the plaintiffs claim that Charles knew two days before a share sale agreement was signed of a deal that would substantially boost the value of the company's oil refinery in Minnesota, said Scott.
Other claims centre on whether Koch broke disclosure rules in accounting for its 1982 earnings, a key factor in valuing the plaintiffs' shares.
Koch Industries representatives did not return phone calls.
"We look forward to a trial on the remaining issues and are confident that we will prevail when all is said and done," Cordes, the Koch executive, said in Tuesday's statement.
A trial is expected in spring or summer of 1998, to be held in federal court in Wichita or Topeka, Scott said.
